content: Radiographic imaging should not be a mandatory requirement or a barrier to initiating tuberculosis (TB) preventive treatment in people living with HIV (PLHIV). This is due to the additional resources required and the minimal improvement in the negative predictive value of such imaging. However, it is important to note that PLHIV with low CD4 counts may still develop active TB even if their chest radiography appears normal. PLHIV who exhibit any of the four key symptoms of TB or have abnormal chest radiographic findings should be evaluated for active TB and other diseases. The Xpert® MTB/RIF test is recommended as the initial diagnostic tool in such cases. Preventive treatment should not be withheld from asymptomatic individuals at risk of TB infection, even if latent TB infection (LTBI) testing or chest radiography is unavailable. For example, PLHIV who are household contacts of TB patients should still be considered for preventive treatment. These investigations should align with national guidelines and sound clinical practices. Contacts who are found not to have active TB should be assessed for eligibility for preventive treatment. Individuals with fibrotic radiological lesions may be at increased risk of disease progression and should be carefully evaluated. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on TB prevention emphasize the importance of follow-up for active TB, even in patients who have completed preventive treatment. For children under 10 years of age, specific symptoms such as persistent cough, fever, weight loss, or growth curve flattening should prompt further evaluation. Asymptomatic infants under one year of age with HIV should only be treated for LTBI if they are household contacts of TB patients. Testing for LTBI using either the tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) can help identify individuals who would benefit most from preventive treatment. However, these tests are not perfect and require a competent immune response to detect TB infection. A positive result does not reliably predict progression to active disease. Both TST and IGRA are considered equivalent options, with advantages and disadvantages depending on the setting. TST may be more familiar and resource-efficient in low-resource settings, but global shortages and stock-outs can limit its availability. IGRA, while more costly and requiring laboratory infrastructure, avoids the booster response seen with TST and requires only a single visit for testing. Preventive treatment options for LTBI include six or nine months of daily isoniazid, a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a three-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. A one-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or four months of daily rifampicin alone may also be considered as alternatives. The choice of regimen depends on factors such as age, drug susceptibility, risk of toxicity, availability, and patient preferences. In high TB transmission settings, PLHIV with unknown or positive LTBI test results who are unlikely to have active TB should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT), regardless of antiretroviral therapy (ART) status, degree of immunosuppression, or pregnancy. This recommendation is based on evidence that longer-term IPT significantly enhances the protective benefits of ART. Drug-drug interactions must be carefully managed when using rifamycin-containing regimens, as these drugs can interfere with the metabolism of other medications, including antiretrovirals, anticoagulants, and oral contraceptives. For example, rifampicin can reduce the concentrations of certain antiretroviral agents, necessitating dose adjustments or alternative regimens. Rifapentine-containing regimens, such as 3HP, can be safely administered with efavirenz-based ART without dose adjustments. All recommended treatment options can be self-administered, which may improve adherence and reduce barriers to implementation. However, patients should have access to advice on managing adverse events and completing treatment. Shorter regimens, such as 3HP or 1HP, are generally preferred by patients and clinicians due to their convenience and higher completion rates. In summary, TB preventive treatment should be tailored to individual risk factors, clinical settings, and available resources, with a focus on maximizing adherence and minimizing barriers to care.
